claim: Gamma activity in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is widely viewed as a pro-kinetic rhythm.
source: Gamma activity in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is widely viewed as a pro-kinetic rhythm.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevailing view in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript and implied citations in the broader literature discussion.

claim: STN gamma (60–90 Hz) increased most strongly when the tap was successfully stopped.
source: STN gamma (60–90 Hz) increased most strongly when the tap was successfully stopped, whereas phase-based connectivity between the contralateral STN and motor cortex decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including figures showing power changes.

claim: Phase-based connectivity between the contralateral STN and motor cortex decreased during successful stopping.
source: STN gamma (60–90 Hz) increased most strongly when the tap was successfully stopped, whereas phase-based connectivity between the contralateral STN and motor cortex decreased.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by connectivity analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The STN receives cortical input via the hyperdirect pathway.
source: The STN is well-positioned to cancel actions as it receives cortical input via the hyperdirect pathway and can inhibit the thalamus and brainstem via the basal ganglia output nuclei as well as the striatum via the globus pallidus externus (GPe) (Mink, 1996; Wei and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The STN can inhibit the thalamus and brainstem via the basal ganglia output nuclei.
source: The STN is well-positioned to cancel actions as it receives cortical input via the hyperdirect pathway and can inhibit the thalamus and brainstem via the basal ganglia output nuclei as well as the striatum via the globus pallidus externus (GPe) (Mink, 1996; Wei and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This anatomical and functional relationship is supported by cited literature.

claim: The STN can inhibit the striatum via the globus pallidus externus (GPe).
source: The STN is well-positioned to cancel actions as it receives cortical input via the hyperdirect pathway and can inhibit the thalamus and brainstem via the basal ganglia output nuclei as well as the striatum via the globus pallidus externus (GPe) (Mink, 1996; Wei and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research.

claim: When rats attempted to cancel an action, increased STN firing activity was found irrespective of whether cancellation was successful or not.
source: When rats attempted to cancel an action, increased STN firing activity was found irrespective of whether cancellation was successful or not (Schmidt et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Micro-electrode recordings in the human STN revealed two distinct subpopulations that selectively increased firing rate either during successful response inhibition or during motor execution.
source: but more recently, micro-electrode recordings in the human STN revealed two distinct subpopulations that selectively increased firing rate either during successful response inhibition or during motor execution (Bastin et al., 2014; Benis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Arkypallidal cells in the GPe have been specifically linked to action cancellation.
source: Also in the GPe a subpopulation termed arkypallidal cells, which seem to receive input not only from the striatum but also from the STN (Nevado-Holgado et al., 2014), has specifically been linked to action cancellation (Mallet et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific research.

claim: Oscillations, particularly in the gamma band (>30 Hz), have been proposed to be a key mechanism for coordinating spatially separate but functionally related assemblies.
source: Oscillations, particularly in the gamma band (>30 Hz), have been proposed to be a key mechanism for coordinating spatially separate but functionally related assemblies (Bosman et al., 2012; Fries, 2015; Nikolić et al., 2013; Schoffelen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: A local field potential study in Parkinson's disease patients has shown increased 55–75 Hz gamma activity when patients failed to stop.
source: A local field potential study in Parkinson's disease patients, however, has shown increased 55–75 Hz gamma activity when patients failed to stop (Alegre et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Gamma activity is pro-kinetic or related to response vigour.
source: which is in line with the prevailing view that gamma activity is pro-kinetic (Cassidy et al., 2002; Fogelson et al., 2005; Litvak et al., 2012) or related to response vigour (Jenkinson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim about the prevailing view is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Beta activity is widely viewed as a marker of broad motor suppression within the STN as well as cortex.
source: Beta activity, instead, is widely viewed as a marker of broad motor suppression within the STN (Wessel et al., 2016a) as well as cortex (Swann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: High STN beta activity was linked to elongated response times during incongruent trials in a Stroop task.
source: High STN beta activity for example was linked to elongated response times during incongruent trials in a Stroop task (Brittain et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: High STN beta activity was linked to stronger suppression of cortico-spinal excitability during speech inhibition.
source: and to stronger suppression of cortico-spinal excitability during speech inhibition (Wessel et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Movements coincide with decreasing beta and increasing gamma activity.
source: However, as movements are known to coincide with decreasing beta and increasing gamma activity (Joundi et al., 2012; Lalo et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: The mean stop signal delay time with a 55% ± (SD) 10% successful stopping rate was 707 ± 49 ms (range = 620–760 ms).
source: The mean stop signal delay time with a 55% ± (SD) 10% successful stopping rate was 707 ± 49 ms (range = 620–760 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data collected in the study.

claim: The mean interval between the preceding tap and the unsuccessfully inhibited tap in trials where stopping failed was 864 ± 36 ms.
source: The mean interval between the preceding tap and the unsuccessfully inhibited tap in trials where stopping failed was 864 ± 36 ms, and was significantly shorter than the 900 ms interval dictated by the metronome (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data with statistical testing.

claim: The mean interval between the preceding tap and the unsuccessfully inhibited tap was significantly shorter than the 900 ms interval dictated by the metronome.
source: The mean interval between the preceding tap and the unsuccessfully inhibited tap in trials where stopping failed was 864 ± 36 ms, and was significantly shorter than the 900 ms interval dictated by the metronome (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of the behavioral data.

claim: In trials where stopping failed, patients would have still had on average 156 ms to stop.
source: In these trials, patients would have still had on average 156 ms to stop.
evidence: This is calculated from the behavioral data presented.

claim: Movement trajectories preceding successfully or unsuccessfully inhibited stops were overlapping.
source: Movement trajectories preceding successfully or unsuccessfully inhibited stops were overlapping (Figure 1, trajectories measured by a pressure sensor and goniometer).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In 7 of 9 subjects, movement extent correlated with the tap-to-sound offset.
source: In 7 of 9 subjects, movement extent correlated with the tap-to-sound offset, which indicates that stopping performance was worse when the foregoing tap was relatively late in a trial corresponding to previous results (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Stopping performance was worse when the foregoing tap was relatively late in a trial.
source: In 7 of 9 subjects, movement extent correlated with the tap-to-sound offset, which indicates that stopping performance was worse when the foregoing tap was relatively late in a trial corresponding to previous results (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: None of the tested variables were associated with successful stopping after FDR-correction of the resulting p-values.
source: However, none of the tested variables were associated with successful stopping after FDR-correction of the resulting p-values (see Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: A surprising sound alone already elicits motor slowing of verbal reports.
source: Previous research suggests that a surprising sound alone already elicits motor slowing of verbal reports (Wessel and Aron, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The median intertap interval directly preceding the stop signal (median ITI = 893 ms) did not differ significantly from the one directly after the stop signal (median ITI = 889 ms) in the control condition.
source: The median intertap interval directly preceding the stop signal (median ITI = 893 ms) did not differ significantly from the one directly after the stop signal (median ITI = 889 ms, Wilcoxon signed-rank test p=1.0).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of behavioral data from the control condition.

claim: The STN contralateral to the tapping hand responded to the stop signal with a 60–90 Hz gamma power increase when compared to activity from the tap before.
source: The STN contralateral to the tapping hand responded to the stop signal with a 60–90 Hz gamma power increase when compared to activity from the tap before (Figure 2.1 shows the reference data from the tap before aligned to where the stop signal would have occurred if it would have been presented one tap earlier; Figure 2.2 shows the response to the stop signal; Figure 3A shows the contrast between the two).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: STN gamma (60–90 Hz) increase was significantly and consistently higher during successful movement inhibition.
source: Importantly, this gamma increase was significantly and consistently higher during successful movement inhibition (Figure 2.3 + 2.4, and 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 3B.

claim: The effect size of the 60–90 Hz power difference between successful and failed stops was very large (Cohen's d meanwinOfInt = 1.2, maxwinOfInt = 2.6).
source: The effect size of this difference was very large (60–90 Hz power difference between successful-failed stops: Cohen's d meanwinOfInt = 1.2, maxwinOfInt = 2.6).
evidence: This is a statistical measure calculated from the data.

claim: During regular tapping, the typical pattern of movement-related gamma power increase and beta power decrease was observed.
source: Note that during regular tapping we observed the typical pattern of movement-related gamma power increase and beta power decrease (Figure 2.1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gamma power increased during both movement execution and movement inhibition.
source: Gamma power thus increased during both movement execution and movement inhibition.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing gamma increases in both conditions.

claim: The movement-related gamma peak was broader and weaker than the stop-related increase that peaked around 70 Hz.
source: The movement-related peak was broader and weaker than the stop-related increase that peaked around 70 Hz (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cortical EEGs recorded a low-frequency increase in response to the stop signal in all channels.
source: Cortical EEGs recorded a low-frequency increase in response to the stop signal in all channels (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The cortical low-frequency increase was not significantly higher during successful stopping.
source: which was – in contrast to STN gamma activity – not significantly higher during successful stopping (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the EEG data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only 8–30 Hz power over contralateral C3/C4, Cz and Fz was significantly higher when stopping was successful.
source: Only 8–30 Hz power over contralateral C3/C4, Cz and Fz was significantly higher when stopping was successful.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the EEG data.

claim: There was no overall power increase following the stop signal in the 8–30 Hz band in C3/C4, Cz and Fz channels when compared to the tap before.
source: However, there was no overall power increase following the stop signal in the 8–30 Hz band in these channels when compared to the tap before (Figure 3A), not even when only successful stop trials were considered (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: No gamma increase was observed in the control condition when stopping was not attempted.
source: Importantly, no gamma increase was observed in this control condition, even though the difference between successful and unsuccessful stops was still significant despite the reduced sample size of 6 patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The difference in gamma power between successful and unsuccessful stops was still significant in the control condition analysis despite the reduced sample size of 6 patients.
source: Importantly, no gamma increase was observed in this control condition, even though the difference between successful and unsuccessful stops was still significant despite the reduced sample size of 6 patients (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the control condition data.

claim: Periods of high gamma activity in the STN have been reported to coincide with an overall increase in firing rate and phase-locking of spikes to the gamma cycle peak.
source: Periods of high gamma activity in the STN have been reported to coincide with an overall increase in firing rate and phase-locking of spikes to the gamma cycle peak (Pogosyan et al., 2006; Trottenberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The strength of gamma synchronization in the STN or its coherence with C3/C4 did not depend on the exact movement performed.
source: After observing that the strength of gamma synchronization in the STN or its coherence with C3/C4 did not depend on the exact movement performed, Litvak and colleagues suggested that STN gamma activity modulates rather than explicitly encodes motor commands (Litvak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: STN gamma activity modulates rather than explicitly encodes motor commands.
source: After observing that the strength of gamma synchronization in the STN or its coherence with C3/C4 did not depend on the exact movement performed, Litvak and colleagues suggested that STN gamma activity modulates rather than explicitly encodes motor commands (Litvak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: STN gamma activity has been linked to effort.
source: This notion is also compatible with observations that have linked STN gamma activity to effort (Jenkinson et al., 2013; Oswal et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2013) and arousal (Brücke et al., 2013; Jenkinson et al., 2013; Kempf et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: STN gamma activity has been linked to arousal.
source: This notion is also compatible with observations that have linked STN gamma activity to effort (Jenkinson et al., 2013; Oswal et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2013) and arousal (Brücke et al., 2013; Jenkinson et al., 2013; Kempf et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Stopping was more likely successful after STN gamma was relatively high already 200 ms before the stop cue.
source: The fact that stopping was more likely successful after STN gamma was relatively high already 200 ms before the stop cue (i.e. before patients knew they had to stop) may reflect such arousal-related function and the need for proactive inhibition.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data showing pre-stop signal gamma differences.

claim: A broad gamma increase was observed during stopping in electrocorticography recordings from the pre-supplementary motor area and right inferior frontal gyrus.
source: However, a broad gamma increase was observed during stopping in electrocorticography recordings from the pre-supplementary motor area and right inferior frontal gyrus (Swann et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Gamma has been reported to be specifically localized in the dorsal part of the STN.
source: However, gamma has been reported to be specifically localized in the dorsal part of the STN (Trottenberg et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Parkinson's disease patients may exhibit pathological STN hyperactivity expressed in abnormal firing rates and patterns.
source: Another limitation of this study is that we recorded from patients that may exhibit pathological STN hyperactivity (Hamani et al., 2004) expressed in abnormal firing rates and patterns (Magnin et al., 2000; Remple et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Pathological changes in STN activity are attenuated by dopaminergic medication.
source: Even though these pathological changes are attenuated by dopaminergic medication (Brown et al., 2001; Heimer et al., 2006; Levy et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Gamma increased most strongly in trials where participants were able to stop fully instead of interrupting the downward movement halfway.
source: Additionally, we observed that gamma increased most strongly in trials where participants were able to stop fully instead of interrupting the downward movement halfway, showing that gamma increased not only during braking in the middle of a movement but that it increased even more in the absence of any movement.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data categorized by movement extent.

claim: Higher post-movement C3/C4 beta activity is linked to subsequently improved stopping performance.
source: As reported previously, we confirmed a link between higher post-movement C3/C4 beta activity and subsequently improved stopping performance, which we suggest was related to fluctuations in cognitive load (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data in the current study and citation to previous work.

claim: Beta has been implicated in time estimation.
source: Beta has also been implicated in time estimation (Kononowicz and van Rijn, 2015)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Stopping success was correlated with the tap-to-sound offset of the last regular tap in seven patients.
source: Stopping success indeed was correlated with the tap-to-sound offset of the last regular tap in seven patients, such that relatively early taps (early with respect to the sound, which should be compensated for by delaying the next tap) were followed by higher stopping success.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Significantly higher beta power was observed over contralateral motor and frontal cortex when stopping was successful in comparison to when it failed.
source: We also observed significantly higher beta power over contralateral motor and frontal cortex when stopping was successful in comparison to when it failed.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the EEG data.

claim: Beta oscillations are less likely to occur during movement execution.
source: As beta oscillations are less likely to occur during movement execution (Feingold et al., 2015; Kilavik et al., 2013), this difference was expected.
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: No beta increase was observed after the stop signal in comparison to the previous regular tap, not even when only successful stop trials were considered.
source: Importantly, in the present study no beta increase was observed after the stop signal in comparison to the previous regular tap – not even when only successful stop trials were considered.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data.

claim: A weaker STN beta decrease was observed during 'proactively inhibited' go-trials in comparison to go-trials with a cue which was never followed by a stop signal.
source: How can we reconcile the above with the results reported by Benis et al. (2014), who observed a weaker STN beta decrease during 'proactively inhibited' go-trials ('proactively inhibited' as participants were aware that a stop signal may come after the cue, although it did not appear in these trials) in comparison to go-trials with a cue, which was never followed by a stop signal and thus resulted in faster reaction times?
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study.

claim: A stronger difference in beta decrease between the two trial types was linked to shorter stop signal reaction times across patients.
source: A stronger difference in beta decrease between the two trial types was also linked to shorter stop signal reaction times across patients.
evidence: This is a description of findings from cited literature.

claim: Elevated beta activity may reflect better connectivity across task-relevant areas.
source: Finally, our results may also be reconciled with those reported by Wessel et al. (2016a) if elevated beta activity reflects better connectivity across task-relevant areas (Gross et al., 2004) or reduced cognitive load (particularly for <20 Hz beta) (Fischer et al., 2016; Rouhinen et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Elevated beta activity may reflect reduced cognitive load.
source: Finally, our results may also be reconciled with those reported by Wessel et al. (2016a) if elevated beta activity reflects better connectivity across task-relevant areas (Gross et al., 2004) or reduced cognitive load (particularly for <20 Hz beta) (Fischer et al., 2016; Rouhinen et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: An STN gamma increase was observed concurrent with response slowing in a verbal working memory task.
source: Recently, an influential hypothesis suggesting that motor suppression is implemented by fronto-central low-frequency activity has received further support (Wessel et al., 2016b). Even though the authors also observed an STN gamma increase concurrent with response slowing, this increase was associated with the cognitive demands of the verbal working memory task rather than motor inhibition.
evidence: This is a description of findings from a cited study.

claim: The auditory stop cue elicited a slow-wave power increase.
source: Similar to classical stop signal tasks, our auditory stop cue also elicited a slow-wave power increase.
evidence: This is based on the data from the current study.

claim: The slow-wave power increase occurred also when stopping was not even attempted in the control condition.
source: However, this increase occurred also when stopping was not even attempted.
evidence: This is based on data from the control condition.

claim: The intertap interval in the control condition between the tap before and the tap immediately after the stop signal was not increased.
source: If the slow-wave power increase over Cz would have induced slowing or braking, then the intertap interval in the control condition between the tap before and the tap immediately after the stop signal should have been increased, and this was not the case.
evidence: This is based on analysis of behavioral data from the control condition.

claim: ISPC of 60–75 Hz gamma between the contralateral motor cortex and the contralateral STN decreased strongly and significantly in response to the stop signal.
source: ISPC of 60–75 Hz gamma between the contralateral motor cortex and the contralateral STN decreased strongly and significantly in response to the stop signal relative to the average of the −350:0 ms window preceding the stop signal (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by connectivity analysis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: An increase of 6–12 Hz ISPC to all cortical channels was observed in response to the stop signal.
source: We also observed an increase of 6–12 Hz ISPC to all cortical channels.
evidence: This is based on connectivity analysis of the data.

claim: If the upcoming tap was inhibited more successfully, STN gamma power was already higher prior to the stop signal.
source: Finally we assessed if gamma power was already tonically elevated prior to the stop signal, before participants knew they had to stop. We tested for significant differences within a 350 ms window before the stop signal. If the upcoming tap was inhibited more successfully, STN gamma power was already higher prior to the stop signal (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: 20–30 Hz beta power over C3/C4 ipsilateral to the tapping hand was significantly higher preceding successful stops.
source: 20–30 Hz beta power over C3/C4 ipsilateral to the tapping hand also was significantly higher preceding successful stops.
evidence: This is based on analysis of pre-stop signal EEG data.

claim: When data were re-aligned to the last regular tap instead of the stop signal, a second significant cluster at 20–30 Hz over C3/C4 contralateral to the tapping hand was found.
source: If the data were re-aligned to the last regular tap instead of the stop signal, a second significant cluster at 20–30 Hz over C3/C4 contralateral to the tapping hand was found, in line with previous reports (Fischer et al., 2016) (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of the data with different alignment, supported by citation.

claim: The average gamma peak of successful stops at 106 ± (SD) 59 ms occurred earlier than the average unsuccessful tap (at 156 ± 50 ms).
source: Indeed, the average gamma peak of successful stops at 106 ± (SD) 59 ms occurred earlier than the average unsuccessful tap (at 156 ± 50 ms), whereas the average gamma peak of failed stops occurred later (at 179 ± 84 ms).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of gamma peaks in the data.

claim: The average gamma peak of failed stops occurred later (at 179 ± 84 ms) than the average unsuccessful tap.
source: Indeed, the average gamma peak of successful stops at 106 ± (SD) 59 ms occurred earlier than the average unsuccessful tap (at 156 ± 50 ms), whereas the average gamma peak of failed stops occurred later (at 179 ± 84 ms).
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of gamma peaks in the data.

claim: Gamma peak timings significantly differed between successful and failed stops (t(8)=-2.9, p=0.019, CIdiff=[−131, –16 ms], Cohen's d = 1.0).
source: These gamma peak timings significantly differed from each other (t(8)=-2.9, p=0.019, CIdiff=[−131, –16 ms], Cohen's d = 1.0).
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of the gamma peak timing data.

claim: Within-subject correlations between movement extent and gamma within the stopping window (0–156 ms) after the stop signal were significant in 8 of 9 patients when gamma was taken from the contralateral STN.
source: We also examined within-subject correlations between movement extent (i.e. inhibition failure) and gamma within the stopping window (0–156 ms) after the stop signal (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This was significant in 8 of 9 patients (uncorrected tests; P3's confidence intervals were borderline significant, Spearman's rho p=0.049) when gamma was taken from the contralateral STN
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In all but one patient, when gamma was higher, movement extent was less and stopping was more successful.
source: meaning that in all but one patient we found that when gamma was higher, movement extent was less and stopping was more successful.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation analysis.

claim: In contralateral C3/C4 and in ipsilateral STN, a correlation between movement extent and gamma was present only in three patients.
source: In contralateral C3/C4 and in ipsilateral STN such a relationship was present only in three patients, and in ipsilateral motor cortex only in one patient, further indicating specificity to the correlation with contralateral STN activity.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis across different recording sites.

claim: In ipsilateral motor cortex, a correlation between movement extent and gamma was present only in one patient.
source: In contralateral C3/C4 and in ipsilateral STN such a relationship was present only in three patients, and in ipsilateral motor cortex only in one patient, further indicating specificity to the correlation with contralateral STN activity.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis across different recording sites.

claim: In full stop trials, gamma increased most strongly.
source: Still, in full stop trials, gamma increased most strongly.
evidence: This is based on analysis of gamma power categorized by movement extent.

claim: Gamma increased moderately for intermediate stops.
source: It increased moderately for intermediate stops and remained flat for failed stops (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gamma remained flat for failed stops.
source: It increased moderately for intermediate stops and remained flat for failed stops (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activity recorded from the first dorsal interosseous muscle suggests an inverse relationship to the gamma increase.
source: As expected, activity recorded from the first dorsal interosseous muscle of the tapping hand (presented to the right in Figure 4—figure supplement 2) suggests an inverse relationship to the gamma increase.
evidence: This is based on EMG data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cortical 3–5 Hz power increase was clearly present in the stop condition.
source: Finally, we examined if the cortical 3–5 Hz power increase, which was clearly present in the stop condition (Figure 3A), was also present in the control condition when movement inhibition was not even attempted.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The 3–5 Hz power trajectory in Cz representing the control condition shows a very similar peak to the stop condition.
source: The grey power trajectory representing the control condition shows a very similar peak in Cz (Figure 4D, n = 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Significance testing within the crucial reaction time window resulted in no significant differences in 3–5 Hz power between the control condition and either failed or successful stopping.
source: Significance testing within the crucial reaction time window (ranging from the stop signal to the average time of the failed tap, 156 ms later) resulted in no significant differences between the control condition and either the power increase during failed or successful stopping.
evidence: This is based on statistical testing of the low-frequency power data.

claim: The direct comparison between failed or successful stops in 3–5 Hz power was not significant.
source: The direct comparison between failed or successful stops was not significant either.
evidence: This is based on statistical testing.

claim: A peak-extraction analysis failed to detect a difference between low-frequency peaks in Cz between successful stops and control condition.
source: Also a peak-extraction analysis failed to detect a difference between low-frequency peaks (Cz successful stops vs. control: t(5)=0.2, p=0.848, CIdiff=[-−205.1, 240.2%]; failed stops vs. control: t(5)=0.5, p=0.641, CIdiff=[−149.4, 220.8%]).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of peak data.

claim: The 3–5 Hz increase only seemed to be reduced in the control condition in Fz and both M1, however this was not significant.
source: The 3–5 Hz increase only seemed to be reduced in the control condition in Fz and both M1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), however this was also not significant.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ten Parkinson's disease patients were recorded after obtaining informed written consent.
source: Ten Parkinson's disease patients (mean disease duration = 8 ± 4 years, mean age = 59 ± 8 years; one left-handed/ambidextrous; two female) were recorded after obtaining informed written consent to take part in this study, which was approved by the local ethics committee (Oxfordshire REC A, 08/H0604/58).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: One patient had to be excluded from the analysis as they intermittently fell asleep during the testing.
source: One patient had to be excluded from the analysis as they intermittently fell asleep during the testing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data exclusion.

claim: All patients underwent bilateral implantation of deep brain stimulation electrodes into the STN two to six days before the recording.
source: All patients underwent bilateral implantation of deep brain stimulation electrodes into the STN two to six days before the recording with the aim to alleviate symptoms through chronic high-frequency deep brain stimulation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the patient procedures.

claim: Patients were tested on medication to ensure task performance and motor function were as normal as possible.
source: Patients were tested on medication to ensure task performance and motor function were as normal as possible, although acknowledging that functional impairments, albeit lessened, still persist in this state.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the testing conditions.

claim: The stop signal was triggered relative to the tap instead of the metronome sound to keep movement variability to a minimum.
source: It was delivered relative to the tap instead of the metronome sound to keep movement variability to a minimum and to prevent the strategy of delaying the tap relative to the metronome sound.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: The stop signal was delivered relative to the tap to prevent the strategy of delaying the tap relative to the metronome sound.
source: It was delivered relative to the tap instead of the metronome sound to keep movement variability to a minimum and to prevent the strategy of delaying the tap relative to the metronome sound.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design rationale.

claim: The actual average stopping probability was 55% ± (SD) 10%.
source: The actual average stopping probability was 55% ± (SD) 10%.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: Six patients were additionally recorded in a control condition to assess if stopping-related activity was linked to active motor inhibition or whether it merely reflected registration of the more salient stop tone.
source: Six patients were additionally recorded in a control condition to assess if stopping-related activity was linked to active motor inhibition or whether it merely reflected registration of the more salient stop tone.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: STN gamma activity may support flexible motor control as it increased during both movement execution and rapid action-stopping.
source: In summary, STN gamma activity may support flexible motor control as it did not only increase during movement execution but also during rapid action-stopping.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in the study.

claim: The stop signal-evoked slow-wave response does not directly correspond to movement inhibition but instead registers salient sensory stimuli and alerts stopping-relevant areas.
source: Our data suggest an alternative account, namely that the stop signal-evoked slow-wave response does not directly correspond to movement inhibition but instead registers salient sensory stimuli and alerts stopping-relevant areas, which in turn may trigger the STN gamma increase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the data and analysis.

claim: The increase in cortico-subthalamic low-frequency connectivity might underpin the sequence of alerting stopping-relevant areas and triggering the STN gamma increase.
source: The increase in cortico-subthalamic low-frequency connectivity might underpin this sequence, enabling the STN to trigger the stopping process.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the connectivity data.

claim: The event-related low-frequency response would be necessary for, but not equivalent to motor suppression per se.
source: The event-related low-frequency response would thus be necessary for, but not equivalent to motor suppression per se.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the role of low-frequency activity.

claim: Gamma oscillations in the contralateral STN were linked to successful stopping.
source: Taken together, our results showed that gamma oscillations in the contralateral STN were linked to successful stopping.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data.

claim: Gamma oscillations in the STN are not simply pro-kinetic, but can also increase during movement termination.
source: This indicates that gamma oscillations in the STN are not simply pro-kinetic, but that they can also increase during movement termination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing gamma increases during stopping.

claim: The observed gamma rhythm may underpin a fast stopping mechanism involving the STN.
source: Though we can only infer an association and not causation from observational recordings, our data suggest that the observed gamma rhythm may underpin a fast stopping mechanism involving the STN.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation acknowledging the correlative nature of the study.

claim: Gamma oscillations seem to support fast changes in processing demands in cortico-basal ganglia networks.
source: Gamma oscillations therefore seem to support fast changes in processing demands not only in cortical but also in cortico-basal ganglia networks in line with theories of gamma synchrony establishing effective, precise and selective neuronal communication (Fries, 2015).
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates the current findings with cited theoretical frameworks.
